title: Potted Crab
subtitle: White and brown crab meat sealed in spiced clarified butter
excerpt: Potted crab is a British preserve in the old sense: white and brown crab meat seasoned with mace, cayenne, and lemon, packed into ramekins and sealed under a layer of clarified butter. It keeps in the fridge for several days and is served cold with hot toast and a wedge of lemon.
sourceNotes: Potted fish and shellfish are a centuries-old British preservation technique. Mrs Beeton, Book of Household Management (1861), Project Gutenberg #10136, includes potted shrimp, crab, and lobster. The method of sealing under clarified butter was standard practice before refrigeration and remains the best version of the dish today.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Potted crab keeps in the fridge for up to 3 days once sealed. The butter seal must remain intact; once broken, eat within a day.

content.text: Potted crab uses both the white and brown meat from a dressed crab. The white meat is delicate and sweet; the brown is rich, intense, and slightly mineral. Together they make a more interesting filling than white meat alone. A seal of clarified butter over the top keeps the crab fresh and, when cold from the fridge, forms a firm disc that breaks cleanly with a knife.

In a bowl, combine the white and brown crab meat with half the lemon juice, the cayenne pepper, the mace, and the salt. Mix gently with a fork until just combined. Taste and adjust the seasoning: the mixture should be well-seasoned and have a noticeable spice. Divide between 4 ramekins, pressing gently to level the top.

Melt {{unsalted-butter}} of butter in a small saucepan over a very low heat without stirring. After 5 minutes, the white milk solids will have settled to the bottom and the clear golden liquid on top is the clarified butter. Very carefully pour the clear layer over each ramekin to cover the crab completely, leaving the milky solids behind in the pan.
Leave to cool at room temperature for 15 minutes, then refrigerate for at least 1 hour until the butter is fully set. Serve with hot toast and lemon wedges.

items.symptom: The butter seal has turned white and grainy
items.cause: The butter was cooled too quickly in the fridge before it set.
items.fix: Allow the potted crab to cool to room temperature at the counter before refrigerating. The butter should set slowly for a smooth, even layer.

items.cause: The seasoning was not adjusted after mixing, or the brown crab meat ratio is too low.
items.fix: Season the mixture well before potting: it should taste slightly over-seasoned at room temperature, as cold temperatures mute flavour. The brown meat adds depth; do not omit it.

items.symptom: The clarified butter contains milky sediment
items.cause: The butter was poured too hastily and the milk solids were disturbed.
items.fix: Pour very slowly and stop well before the milky layer at the bottom. A ladle is easier to control than tipping the pan.

content.text: Potting under butter is a preservation technique that predates refrigeration: the sealed fat layer excludes air and slows spoilage. For crab and shrimp it remains the best way to serve the meat cold, because the spiced butter melts as it warms and seasons each bite. Potted shrimp from Morecambe Bay is perhaps the best-known British example; potted crab, using the larger and more intensely flavoured meat of the brown crab, is a close rival. It is most often served as a starter or a lunch dish with good toast and a simple green salad.
